caption.text: 1	NASA sent 2,478 baby jellyfish to space in 1991. They came back as 60,000 — and every single one born in orbit could never swim straight again. Jellyfish sense gravity the same way humans do. In space, these senses formed differently. And there was no fixing it after. Which means gravity isn’t just something we’re used to. It’s something we need — during development — to build a brain that can function on Earth. So here’s the question NASA was actually asking: If a child is born on a space station or Mars colony and grows up in microgravity… can they ever come home? We don’t have the answer for humans yet. But the Jellyfish experiment says no. Perhaps artificial gravity might be the solution however, this has not been tested yet.

caption.text:
Your stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal.
And somehow… it keeps you alive.

Your stomach runs on hydrochloric acid with a pH near 1.
That’s strong enough to break down steel, sanitize food, and dissolve bones.

This acid isn’t a flaw. It’s a weapon.
It kills pathogens. Unlocks nutrients. Turns food into fuel.

But here’s the problem.

Your stomach is built to hold acid.
Your esophagus is not.

After a heavy, fatty, or acidic meal, pressure builds.
The valve relaxes. Acid escapes upward.

That burn? That’s stomach acid touching tissue it was never meant to reach.

This isn’t your body failing.
It’s your body overflowing.

So here’s how to work with the system:
❌ STOP: Overloading your stomach late at night with huge, heavy meals
✅ START: Smaller portions, upright posture, and giving digestion time

Antacids don’t “fix” acid.
They buffer it—just enough to protect the wrong tissue.

Your stomach acid is incredible.
Just make sure it stays where it belongs.

@Science is wild. Follow for more videos like this!
